nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
June 7, 1990.  Thomas Czapla; NOAA SEA Division

FLELMR CODE: 5588

Common Name:  Brown Shrimp
Scientific Name:  Penaeus aztecus
Other Common Names: Brownies; Golden shrimp; Green lake shrimp; Northern brown shrimp; Native shrimp; Red or red tail shrimp (495).

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Kingdom: Animalia
	Phylum: Arthropoda
	Class: Malacostraca
	Order: Decapoda
	Family: Penaeidae

Note: Reference for scientific name = Ives
	Subphylum: Crustacea

nodes.title: Value
nodes.body:
Commercial:   The Gulf of Mexico shrimp fishery is the most valuable commercial fishery in the U.S.  Total brown shrimp production for the area west of the Mississippi River Delta to the Texas-Mexico border was 67.7 million pounds heads-off in 1985; slightly higher than the average yield of 67.1 million pounds from 1976-1984 (384).  The season begins in May, peaks from June to July and gradually declines through April.  Major fishing grounds are off the coasts of Texas and Louisiana.  Federal regulations have annually closed the offshore fishery along the coast of Texas from around mid-May to mid-July not more than 55 days to allow shrimp to grow to larger sizes (385 384).  The majority of the brown shrimp are harvested for human consumption.  In addition a bait-shrimp fishery also exists (384).

Recreational:   Approximately 8.8 and 5.2 million lbs (heads on) of total shrimp were taken by recreational shrimpers in 1979 and 1980, respectively, in Texas and Louisiana.  In Louisiana, no license is required for otter trawls up to 16 ft.  In Texas, licenses are required for recreational fishermen, in addition, a license is needed for trawls; catches are limited by location and season of fishing (250).

Indicator:  Miligan (469) indicated dredge material was non-toxic to brown shrimp when exposed to dredge material free of significant concentrations of heavy metals, pesticides and waste metabolites.  A second experimental phase demonstrated better growth for shrimp from dredge material treated ponds, compounding factors eliminated direct results from a third experiment in dredge material containment site.  Ward et al. (755) determined a concentration of 1.2 mg/l selenium (96 h LC50) to be toxic to brown shrimp.  Wofford et al. (772) observed the bioaccumulation of phthalate esters (plasticizers) and demonstrated brown shrimp were better biodegraders of the ester than oysters.

Ecological role:  Brown shrimp are consumed by many finfish species and by large crustaceans.  The loss of marsh habitat and reduction in freshwater inflow into the bays have come under recent scrutiny, as major influencing factors on shrimp production (396 476 787).

nodes.title: Range
nodes.body:
Overall:  Penaeus aztecus is distributed from Martha`s Vinyard, Massachusetts, around the tip of Florida and throughout the Gulf of Mexico to northwestern Yucatan.  They are conspicuously absent along the western Florida coast from the Sanibel grounds to Appalachicola Bay.  Their maximum density occurs along the coasts of Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi (767 681).

Within Study Area:  In the northwest Gulf of Mexico, brown shrimp are distributed through out bays, estuaries and coastal waters.  In the estuaries, postlarvae and small juveniles are associated with shallow vegetated habitats and large juveniles-subadults inhabiting non-vegetated, deeper open water bottoms (539 787).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Brown shrimp have an annual life cycle (545).
Eggs are denser than seawater and demersal (396).
Larva: Larval stages are planktonic, their position in the water column is dependent on time of day, water temperature and clarity (718 719 397).  Fall-spawned postlarvae may burrow into the sediments to escape cooler temperatures and overwinter (669 8).
Juveniles: Postlarvae move into estuaries and transform into benthic juveniles (411).
Adults generally inhabit offshore waters ranging from 14 to 110 meters (589).

Habitat Type:  Eggs occur offshore and are semi-buoyant. Larvae occur offshore and begin to immigrate to estuaries as postlarvae around 8-14 mm TL (411).  Juveniles and subadults prefer shallow, marsh areas and estuarine bays.  Adults occur in neritic Gulf waters (545 767).

Substrate:  Larvae and juveniles inhabit soft, muddy areas, especially in association with plant-water interfaces.  Adults are associated with terrigenous silt and muddy sand substrate (767 303).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature:  Eggs will not hatch at temperatures below 24 C (411).  Postlarvae have been collected from temperatures of 12.6-30.6 C.  Aldrich et al. (8) demonstrated postlarval burrowing in temperatures below 18 C.  The amount of time spent in temperatures below 20 C may be detrimental to population survival (785).  Brown shrimp greater than 75 mm tolerate temperatures between 4 and 36 C with a preferred range of 14.9-31.0 C (755).

Salinity: Brown shrimp are euryhaline to stenohaline depending on life-stage.  Larvae tolerate salinities ranging from 24.1-36 ppt (Cook and Murphy 1966).  Postlarvae have been collected from salinities of 0.1-69 ppt and have good growth at 2-40 ppt.  Juvenile brown shrimp are distributed over 0-45 ppt, but prefer  10-20 ppt.  Adults tolerate salinities of 0.8-45 ppt with an optimum range of 24-38.9 ppt.  Salinity and temperature effects are more conspicuous at either extreme (785).

Migrations and Movements: Brown shrimp and postlarvae move into estuaries from February to April with the incoming tides (138 379).  In the northern Gulf of Mexico, estuarine recruitment may occur all year (37).  Emigration to offshore spawning grounds occurs from May through August, coinciding with full moons and ebb tides (134).  Tagging studies in the northern Gulf indicate a west- and southward movement of the adults with the prevailing currents (411); however more recent studies do not indicate any net movement in any direction (P. Sheridan, per. comm).

nodes.title: Reproduction
nodes.body:
Repro Mode:  Sexual reproduction with external fertilization (411 861).

Mating and Spawning:  In waters off Texas, spawning occurs at depths greater than 14 m; year-round at depths of 64-110 m; and in shallower water peaks of spawning are during late spring and in the fall (589).  Brown shrimp may spawn more than once (545).  Spawning is usually at night (298).

Reproductive captivity:  Reitsema, et al. (1982) found brown shrimp released an average of 246,000 viable eggs of which 15 % hatched.

Growth and Development
Eggs:   Eggs are approximately 0.26 mm in diameter.  Hatch occurs within 24 hours of release into the water column (396).

Larval and Juvenile:  Larvae transform through 5 naupliar stages with average total lengths of 0.35, 0.39, 0.40, 0.44 and 0.50 mm respectively; 3 protozoeal stages, average total lengths of 0.96, 1.71, and 2.59; and 3 myses stages, average total lengths of 3.3, 3.8 and 4.3 to become postlarvae at an average total length of 4.6, in a period of 10-25 days (Cook and Murphy 1969).  Postlarvae enter the estuaries and transform into juveniles around 25 mm TL.

Juveniles: in the estuary range from approximately 25-90 mm.  The shrimp spend approximately 3 months on the nursery grounds and then move back offshore in sizes ranging from 80-100 mm TL (Cook and Linder 1970; 134 539).  Growth rates are temperature dependent. Larval growth rate estimates: nauplii, 0.1-0.2 mm/day; protozoe 0.3-0.35 mm/day; myses 0.4-0.5 mm/day (755).  Postlarval growth is maximum between 25-27 C, greater than 0.5 mm/day.  Juveniles have grown at 3.3 mm/day at temperatures above 25 C; growth decreases from 29-33 C (785).  Growth of offshore adults has not been studied in detail.

Adults:  Females usually reach sexual maturity at ca. 140 mm TL (298).

Food and Feeding
All life stages are omnivorous, feeding begins with the first protozoeal stage (Cook and Murphy 1969).  Larval stages feed on phytoplankton and zooplankton.  Postlarvae feed on epiphytes, phytoplankton and detritus, better growth is attained on animal food (785). Juveniles and adults forage nocturnally on available food progressing from encounter-feeders to selective omnivore-predators ingesting: polychaetes, amphipods, chrironomid larvae, but also detritus and algae (250 785).

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
June 7, 1990.  Thomas Czapla; NOAA SEA Division

FLELMR CODE: 5588

Common Name:  Brown Shrimp
Scientific Name:  Penaeus aztecus
Other Common Names: Brownies; Golden shrimp; Green lake shrimp; Northern brown shrimp; Native shrimp; Red or red tail shrimp (495).

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Kingdom: Animalia
	Phylum: Arthropoda
	Class: Malacostraca
	Order: Decapoda
	Family: Penaeidae

Note: Reference for scientific name = Ives
	Subphylum: Crustacea

sections.heading: Value
sections.content:
Commercial:   The Gulf of Mexico shrimp fishery is the most valuable commercial fishery in the U.S.  Total brown shrimp production for the area west of the Mississippi River Delta to the Texas-Mexico border was 67.7 million pounds heads-off in 1985; slightly higher than the average yield of 67.1 million pounds from 1976-1984 (384).  The season begins in May, peaks from June to July and gradually declines through April.  Major fishing grounds are off the coasts of Texas and Louisiana.  Federal regulations have annually closed the offshore fishery along the coast of Texas from around mid-May to mid-July not more than 55 days to allow shrimp to grow to larger sizes (385 384).  The majority of the brown shrimp are harvested for human consumption.  In addition a bait-shrimp fishery also exists (384).

Recreational:   Approximately 8.8 and 5.2 million lbs (heads on) of total shrimp were taken by recreational shrimpers in 1979 and 1980, respectively, in Texas and Louisiana.  In Louisiana, no license is required for otter trawls up to 16 ft.  In Texas, licenses are required for recreational fishermen, in addition, a license is needed for trawls; catches are limited by location and season of fishing (250).

Indicator:  Miligan (469) indicated dredge material was non-toxic to brown shrimp when exposed to dredge material free of significant concentrations of heavy metals, pesticides and waste metabolites.  A second experimental phase demonstrated better growth for shrimp from dredge material treated ponds, compounding factors eliminated direct results from a third experiment in dredge material containment site.  Ward et al. (755) determined a concentration of 1.2 mg/l selenium (96 h LC50) to be toxic to brown shrimp.  Wofford et al. (772) observed the bioaccumulation of phthalate esters (plasticizers) and demonstrated brown shrimp were better biodegraders of the ester than oysters.

Ecological role:  Brown shrimp are consumed by many finfish species and by large crustaceans.  The loss of marsh habitat and reduction in freshwater inflow into the bays have come under recent scrutiny, as major influencing factors on shrimp production (396 476 787).

sections.heading: Range
sections.content:
Overall:  Penaeus aztecus is distributed from Martha`s Vinyard, Massachusetts, around the tip of Florida and throughout the Gulf of Mexico to northwestern Yucatan.  They are conspicuously absent along the western Florida coast from the Sanibel grounds to Appalachicola Bay.  Their maximum density occurs along the coasts of Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi (767 681).

Within Study Area:  In the northwest Gulf of Mexico, brown shrimp are distributed through out bays, estuaries and coastal waters.  In the estuaries, postlarvae and small juveniles are associated with shallow vegetated habitats and large juveniles-subadults inhabiting non-vegetated, deeper open water bottoms (539 787).

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Brown shrimp have an annual life cycle (545).
Eggs are denser than seawater and demersal (396).
Larva: Larval stages are planktonic, their position in the water column is dependent on time of day, water temperature and clarity (718 719 397).  Fall-spawned postlarvae may burrow into the sediments to escape cooler temperatures and overwinter (669 8).
Juveniles: Postlarvae move into estuaries and transform into benthic juveniles (411).
Adults generally inhabit offshore waters ranging from 14 to 110 meters (589).

Habitat Type:  Eggs occur offshore and are semi-buoyant. Larvae occur offshore and begin to immigrate to estuaries as postlarvae around 8-14 mm TL (411).  Juveniles and subadults prefer shallow, marsh areas and estuarine bays.  Adults occur in neritic Gulf waters (545 767).

Substrate:  Larvae and juveniles inhabit soft, muddy areas, especially in association with plant-water interfaces.  Adults are associated with terrigenous silt and muddy sand substrate (767 303).

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical
sections.content:
Temperature:  Eggs will not hatch at temperatures below 24 C (411).  Postlarvae have been collected from temperatures of 12.6-30.6 C.  Aldrich et al. (8) demonstrated postlarval burrowing in temperatures below 18 C.  The amount of time spent in temperatures below 20 C may be detrimental to population survival (785).  Brown shrimp greater than 75 mm tolerate temperatures between 4 and 36 C with a preferred range of 14.9-31.0 C (755).

Salinity: Brown shrimp are euryhaline to stenohaline depending on life-stage.  Larvae tolerate salinities ranging from 24.1-36 ppt (Cook and Murphy 1966).  Postlarvae have been collected from salinities of 0.1-69 ppt and have good growth at 2-40 ppt.  Juvenile brown shrimp are distributed over 0-45 ppt, but prefer  10-20 ppt.  Adults tolerate salinities of 0.8-45 ppt with an optimum range of 24-38.9 ppt.  Salinity and temperature effects are more conspicuous at either extreme (785).

Migrations and Movements: Brown shrimp and postlarvae move into estuaries from February to April with the incoming tides (138 379).  In the northern Gulf of Mexico, estuarine recruitment may occur all year (37).  Emigration to offshore spawning grounds occurs from May through August, coinciding with full moons and ebb tides (134).  Tagging studies in the northern Gulf indicate a west- and southward movement of the adults with the prevailing currents (411); however more recent studies do not indicate any net movement in any direction (P. Sheridan, per. comm).

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.content:
Repro Mode:  Sexual reproduction with external fertilization (411 861).

Mating and Spawning:  In waters off Texas, spawning occurs at depths greater than 14 m; year-round at depths of 64-110 m; and in shallower water peaks of spawning are during late spring and in the fall (589).  Brown shrimp may spawn more than once (545).  Spawning is usually at night (298).

Reproductive captivity:  Reitsema, et al. (1982) found brown shrimp released an average of 246,000 viable eggs of which 15 % hatched.

Growth and Development
Eggs:   Eggs are approximately 0.26 mm in diameter.  Hatch occurs within 24 hours of release into the water column (396).

Larval and Juvenile:  Larvae transform through 5 naupliar stages with average total lengths of 0.35, 0.39, 0.40, 0.44 and 0.50 mm respectively; 3 protozoeal stages, average total lengths of 0.96, 1.71, and 2.59; and 3 myses stages, average total lengths of 3.3, 3.8 and 4.3 to become postlarvae at an average total length of 4.6, in a period of 10-25 days (Cook and Murphy 1969).  Postlarvae enter the estuaries and transform into juveniles around 25 mm TL.

Juveniles: in the estuary range from approximately 25-90 mm.  The shrimp spend approximately 3 months on the nursery grounds and then move back offshore in sizes ranging from 80-100 mm TL (Cook and Linder 1970; 134 539).  Growth rates are temperature dependent. Larval growth rate estimates: nauplii, 0.1-0.2 mm/day; protozoe 0.3-0.35 mm/day; myses 0.4-0.5 mm/day (755).  Postlarval growth is maximum between 25-27 C, greater than 0.5 mm/day.  Juveniles have grown at 3.3 mm/day at temperatures above 25 C; growth decreases from 29-33 C (785).  Growth of offshore adults has not been studied in detail.

Adults:  Females usually reach sexual maturity at ca. 140 mm TL (298).

Food and Feeding
All life stages are omnivorous, feeding begins with the first protozoeal stage (Cook and Murphy 1969).  Larval stages feed on phytoplankton and zooplankton.  Postlarvae feed on epiphytes, phytoplankton and detritus, better growth is attained on animal food (785). Juveniles and adults forage nocturnally on available food progressing from encounter-feeders to selective omnivore-predators ingesting: polychaetes, amphipods, chrironomid larvae, but also detritus and algae (250 785).
